..
As of 215 PM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: After a beautiful first half of the weekend, tonight 
will mark the transition to a more unsettled weather pattern with 
strengthening gusty southerly winds and multiple rounds of showers 
and some embedded thunderstorms expected through Sunday night/Monday 
morning. 

As surface high pressure shifts east of our area tonight, 
strengthening southerly return flow will transport the higher PW air 
mass (currently over the Mid-Atlantic states) northward into our 
forecast area.  Precipitable water values will increase from around 
0.6 inch today to 1.50-1.75 inches tonight. Gusty southerly winds 
will continue to increase through the day today, especially 
channeled up the Champlain Valley. With relatively warmer Lake 
Champlain temperatures, forecast soundings are indicating enough
mixing is maintained below a low-level temperature inversion to
support Lake Champlain winds of 25 to 30+ knots overnight 
tonight. A Lake Wind Advisory is in effect for Lake Champlain, 
with winds expected to increase this evening and peak overnight 
between midnight and sunrise. Outside of the Lake, expect gusty 
winds 15 to 25 mph over the Champlain Valley, and 10 to 20 mph 
elsewhere. Higher peaks will see gusts 45+ mph tonight. 

A southern stream upper-level shortwave moving through overnight 
will prompt the development of some showers tonight, with an 
embedded thunderstorm or two possible due to some elevated 
instability.  Up to 500 J/kg MUCAPE is progged overnight, highest 
over our western counties in northern NY where the better chances 
for a rumble of thunder exist.  Outside of low thunderstorm 
potential over northern NY, best chances for showers tonight will be 
across southern Vermont, with lower probabilities further north 
towards the International Border.

KEY MESSAGE 2:  During the day on Sunday, some rain showers will linger 
over eastern and southern Vermont during the morning hours as the 
system mentioned in Key Message 1 gradually exits to our east. 
Meanwhile, most areas will then see a break in precipitation during 
the day before the next system moves in from the west.  This next 
system will be supported by strong dynamics as a potent shortwave 
and associated cold front move into the region.  

At this time, it continues to appear that the ingredients will not 
line up ideally to support the development of widespread storms 
later Sunday, though changes in the timing of the system and degree 
of destabilization could increase the thunderstorm potential. 
Current forecast has the break in rain during the day Sunday 
that will allow between 500 and 1000 J/kg SBCAPE to develop 
during the afternoon. However, the better forcing and dynamics 
do not arrive until the early overnight hours, after the peak of
diurnal instability. Therefore, the most likely scenario is 
some scattered showers with a few embedded thunderstorms during 
the afternoon, with higher confidence in a brief round of a 
wetting rain overnight for most areas as the stronger forcing 
moves in. Additional thunderstorms cannot be ruled out 
overnight, but instability will be limited and primarily 
elevated. This will limit the severe threat, though any 
thunderstorms that do develop Sunday or Sunday night could 
produce gusty winds and clou-to-ground lightning, especially 
given the stronger background flow already in place. The Storm 
Prediction Center maintains a Marginal Risk of severe weather 
for much of our area on the latest Day 2 Convective Outlook. 

Conditions will trend drier Monday as high pressure builds in.

KEY MESSAGE 3: High pressure crests Monday night with ideal raditional 
cooling likely. Temperatures in the Adirondacks and northeastern 
Vermont are favored to cool into the mid/upper 30s supporting frost 
potential. Otherwise, 500 mb flow in the mid-high latitudes are 
favored to be mainly zonal with Arctic air trapped well north of the 
region keeping conditions near seasonal levels. Fast-moving troughs 
will be moving through this flow with model trends maintaining a 
weaker wave passing Tuesday night into Wednesday. Latest trends 
continue to point to another wave Thursday into Friday with models 
more consolidated resulting in higher probability of measurable 
rainfall in this time period. Some model guidance keep the surface 
boundary in the vicinity of Vermont/northern New York into the 
weekend with WPC hanging onto 20-40% chances of showers before 
another wave likely moves through sometime over next weekend. The 
main take away here is that there periods of showers with 
temperatures near seasonal levels during the day and above average 
overnight due to pervasive cloud cover.
